To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
genetic variation in neutrophilia is not mediated by macrophages, and that the genetic variation observed in neutrophilia may be mediated by endothelial adhesion molecule expression.
genetic variation of induced peritioneal neutrophilia is not mediated through inflammatory macrophages or by the cytokines IL‐1,IL‐3, GM-CSF, G-CSF and IFN‐γ.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic variation of the inflammatory response to bacterial endotoxin.
the genetic control of neutrophil accumulation and the mechanisms involved in the recruitment of neutrophils to sites of inflammation.
the genetic control of neutrophilia and macrophage responses to inflammatory stimuli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the variation of neutrophil accumulation observed in mice is not due to variation in the number or activity of regulatory cells, nor is it mediated by the cytokines IL‐3, TNF‐α, GM‐CSF, G‐CSF and IFN‐γ, but rather it is due to variation of the expression of endothelial cell adhesion molecules.
the genetic variation in neutrophilia in these mice was not mediated by any of the immune cells or cytokines tested.
genetic variation in neutrophilia is not mediated through a single mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the genetic variation in the magnitude of neutrophil accumulation observed in mice is not due to the presence of regulatory T cells in the circulation, but rather is due to a genetically controlled differential response of the endothelium.
genetic variation in neutrophilia is not mediated through the transfer of inflammatory macro-phages or by the production of cytokines.
there is no evidence for a role of macrophages or cytokines in the genetic control of neutrophil accumulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic variation in the neutrophil accumulation is not mediated through immune cells.

genetic differences in the magnitude of neutrophil responses in mice are not due to variation in the production of neutrophil chemotaxis, but rather due to differences in the ability of the host to attract and/or retain neutrophils at the site of inflammation.
the genetic variation of the inflammatory response in mice is not a consequence of differences in the ability of macrophages to recruit neutrophils.
